subject: ent
title: Le Fort and Midface Fractures and CSF Rhinorrhoea

steps.tx: **Le Fort fractures** classify midface separation injuries by the horizontal level at which the facial skeleton detaches from the skull base after high energy trauma. All types share fracture through the pterygoid plates posteriorly, a detail that confirms the pattern on computed tomography. Airway obstruction from the displaced floating segment, severe bleeding and associated skull base injury dominate the first hours of care.
steps.say: Midface separation injuries classify by the horizontal level of detachment from the skull base. Every pattern shares broken pterygoid plates posteriorly, confirming diagnosis on scanning quickly. Airway compromise and bleeding dominate early care before fixation planning begins.

vis.alt: Anterior skull diagram showing Le Fort fracture lines and orbital floor blowout patterns.
vis.caption: Le Fort fracture lines and orbital blowout patterns. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Le Fort one is a low horizontal fracture above the dental roots separating the alveolus and palate as a floating dentoalveolar segment, with lip swelling and malocclusion. Le Fort two is pyramidal, crossing the nasal bridge, medial orbits and infraorbital rims to produce periorbital oedema, epistaxis and possible cerebrospinal leak. **Guerin sign**, bruising over the palate near the greater palatine vessels, supports a Le Fort pattern clinically.
steps.say: Low fractures free the tooth bearing palate while pyramidal fractures cross the nose and lower orbital rims. Palatal bruising near the greater palatine vessels supports the pattern at bedside examination. Cerebrospinal leakage risk rises as fracture level climbs toward the skull base.

steps.tx: The highest pattern, **craniofacial disjunction**, detaches the entire facial skeleton from the cranium in one block. Fractures run through the nasofrontal junction, orbital walls and zygomaticofrontal sutures, again including the pterygoid plates behind. The face looks elongated and dish-like, with bruising ringing both eyes. Leaking cerebrospinal fluid, lost smell and threatened vision make airway control and urgent specialist care the priorities.
steps.say: Complete separation of face from cranium elongates the face with bruising around both eyes. Spinal fluid leakage with smell loss and eye injury is frequent in this highest pattern.

vis.alt: Skull diagram of Le Fort three injury with fracture lines crossing the zygomaticofrontal sutures and nasal root, separating the whole face from the cranium.
vis.caption: In craniofacial disjunction the facial skeleton hangs detached from the skull base, lengthening the face and bruising both orbits. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Le Fort three is **craniofacial disjunction**, where the entire face separates from the cranium through zygomaticofrontal sutures, nasofrontal junction and orbital walls, producing an elongated dish face with bilateral periorbital haematomas. Cerebrospinal rhinorrhoea, anosmia and ocular injury accompany this highest pattern most often. Mixed asymmetric patterns are commoner than textbook purity, so each side is described independently on imaging reports.
steps.say: Complete separation of face from cranium elongates the face with bruising around both eyes. Spinal fluid leakage with smell loss and eye injury is frequent in this highest pattern. Real injuries mix levels between sides, so imaging describes each side independently.

vis.alt: Diagram of Le Fort one, two and three fractures on a skull with CT of orbital blowout and retrobulbar haemorrhage management.
vis.caption: Le Fort patterns with blowout and haemorrhage management. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The **zygomatic tripod fracture** disrupts the cheek bone at its frontal, maxillary, temporal and sphenoid articulations after direct lateral blows, flattening the malar eminence with subconjunctival haemorrhage, infraorbital numbness and trismus when the arch impinges on coronoid movement. Diplopia signals orbital floor involvement needing ophthalmic assessment. Undisplaced fractures without functional deficit may observe, while displaced fractures need elevation and fixation.
steps.say: Cheek bone injury produces flattening of the malar prominence with numbness below the eye characteristically. Limited mouth opening follows when the arch blocks jaw movement during opening attempts. Double vision indicates orbital involvement that needs formal eye assessment promptly.

steps.tx: A **blow-out fracture** traps the orbital floor after a blunt globe impact raises intraorbital pressure and fractures the thin floor into the maxillary sinus, herniating fat and sometimes inferior rectus muscle. Upward gaze restriction, diplopia, enophthalmos and infraorbital numbness follow, while children may show a trapdoor fracture with vagal nausea despite a white quiet eye. Muscle entrapment in children is a surgical emergency measured in hours.
steps.say: Blunt globe impact usually breaks the thin orbital floor downward into the maxillary sinus below. Trapped fat or muscle restricts upward gaze and produces double vision on looking up. Childhood trapdoor injuries with nausea need release within hours despite a quiet eye.

steps.tx: **Naso-orbito-ethmoid fractures** shatter the central midface bearing the medial canthal tendon, producing telecanthus with a sunken nasal bridge, epiphora from lacrimal injury and frequent cerebrospinal leakage. The canthal bearing fragment decides classification and repair complexity, and tendon reattachment must be precise or the intercanthal widening persists permanently. Associated frontal sinus and skull base injuries are actively excluded by dedicated imaging in every case.
steps.say: Central midface shattering widens the space between the eyes and sinks the nasal bridge visibly. Tear drainage injury adds watering while skull base fracture adds fluid leakage risk concurrently. Precise tendon reattachment decides whether widening persists permanently after healing.

steps.tx: **Mandible fractures** favour the condyle, angle and parasymphysis, often in pairs because the jaw behaves as a bony ring that breaks at two sites after one impact. Malocclusion is the cardinal sign, with step deformity, gingival tears, mental numbness and anterior open bite from bilateral condylar injuries. Airway risk rises with bilateral parasymphyseal fractures that let the tongue fall backward unsupported.
steps.say: Ring behaviour makes the jaw fracture at two sites after a single impact commonly. Bite disturbance is the headline finding alongside step deformity and chin numbness on examination. Bilateral front fractures remove tongue support backward and threaten the airway directly.

steps.tx: **CSF rhinorrhoea** is clear watery unilateral discharge after trauma, surgery or spontaneously, that increases on leaning forward or straining and leaves a salty taste. The halo or double ring sign on filter paper suggests it at the bedside but proves nothing, since blood mixed with tears or discharge mimics it. Beta two transferrin assay of collected fluid is the confirmatory laboratory test used in modern practice.
steps.say: Clear watery one sided discharge worsening on leaning forward suggests spinal fluid leakage post trauma. Ring signs on paper suggest but never prove the diagnosis reliably at bedside. Specific transferrin testing of collected fluid confirms leakage in modern practice.

steps.tx: Leak localisation combines high resolution computed tomography for bony defects with magnetic resonance cisternography for fluid columns, while **intrathecal fluorescent dye** during endoscopy pinpoints elusive intermittent leaks in theatre. The cribriform plate and sphenoid sinus roof are the commonest sites after trauma and surgery respectively. Most traumatic leaks close with bed rest, head elevation and avoidance of straining within a week, reserving repair for persistent, recurrent or meningitis complicated leaks.
steps.say: Bone scanning and fluid sensitive resonance imaging localise most leaks before theatre exploration. Fluorescent dye injected around the cord pinpoints intermittent leaks endoscopically during surgery itself. Traumatic leaks usually seal with rest and head elevation within a week.

steps.tx: **Endoscopic repair** closes confirmed defects with layered grafts of fascia, cartilage or mucosal flaps sealed from inside the nose, succeeding in over ninety percent of first attempts in experienced hands. Lumbar drainage and prophylactic antibiotics remain selective rather than routine companions to repair. Meningitis risk, not discharge volume, is the reason persistent leaks cannot simply be observed forever without a closure plan.
steps.say: Layered grafts placed endoscopically close confirmed defects with success above ninety percent initially. Spinal drainage and preventive antibiotics accompany repair selectively rather than routinely nowadays. Meningitis risk rather than discharge volume justifies closing persistent leaks definitively.

cards.b: All types fracture the pterygoid plates; level rises from alveolus (one) to pyramidal (two) to craniofacial disjunction (three).
Child trapdoor with muscle entrapment and vagal symptoms needs release within hours despite a white eye.
Beta two transferrin in collected fluid; halo sign only suggests. Localise with CT plus MR, repair endoscopically if persistent.

keys: Malocclusion is the cardinal mandible fracture sign
Telecanthus means naso-orbito-ethmoid fracture until disproved
Persistent CSF leak risks meningitis and needs repair
